title: What is the difference between linear search O(n) and binary search O(log n): linear checks every element one by one; binary cuts the search space in half each time but needs sorted data.
shortTitle: Difference Between Linear Search O(n) and Binary Search O(log n)
keyPoints: Linear search scans every element sequentially and works on any data, sorted or unsorted, in O(n) time.
Binary search halves the range each step and requires sorted data, running in O(log n) time.
For one million elements, linear search may need one million comparisons; binary search needs about twenty.
If you search only once, linear scan can be cheaper overall than sorting O(n log n) plus binary search.
For repeated searches on the same data, sort once and binary search many times is the winning strategy.
HashMap gives O(1) average lookups when ordering and range queries are not needed.
Java uses Arrays.sort plus Arrays.binarySearch for sorted-array lookups, or HashMap for hash-based lookups.

s1_definition.oneliner: Linear search checks every element and needs no order; binary search halves a sorted range and is far faster.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Linear search** – examines elements one at a time from the start until the target is found or the collection is exhausted, giving O(n) time.
- **Binary search** – requires sorted data and halves the range each step by comparing the middle element, giving O(log n) time.
- **Precondition trade-off** – binary search is far faster but pays the upfront cost of keeping data sorted.
- **Amortised cost** – sorting once and searching many times amortises the O(n log n) sort cost across all lookups.
- **Access pattern** – linear search works on linked lists and streams; binary search requires random access like arrays.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose you are looking for Rajesh's account in a stack of files at the National Bank of India. Linear search is reading every file from the top of the pile one by one until you hit his, which is simple and works even if the pile is a mess, but slow if the pile is huge. Binary search is like using a sorted filing cabinet: you jump to the middle drawer, decide whether Rajesh is before or after, and keep halving. It is lightning fast, but only works because someone kept the cabinet sorted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Linear search and binary search solve the same problem of finding a target but make opposite trade-offs. Linear search checks elements one at a time from the start and works on any data, sorted or not, in O(n) time. Binary search requires sorted data and halves the range each step, running in O(log n) time. For one million elements, linear search may need one million comparisons while binary search needs only about twenty.

The subtlety is the amortised cost. Binary search is faster per query, but keeping data sorted costs O(n log n). If you search a collection only once, a linear scan is cheaper overall. If you search the same collection many times, you sort once and enjoy logarithmic lookups forever, which is exactly why databases maintain sorted indexes.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, the choice depends on the access pattern. For a one-off audit of unsorted transaction records, linear scan is the right tool. For the sorted account ledger queried thousands of times per second, binary search is indispensable. And when only key-value lookups are needed without ordering, a `HashMap` with O(1) average time often beats both.

The senior-level answer is that choosing correctly among linear search, binary search, HashMap, and TreeMap based on data characteristics and access patterns is what the interviewer is really testing.

Remember one sentence: linear search is O(n) on anything, binary search is O(log n) on sorted data, and matching the tool to the access pattern is the real skill.
